title: Mechanobiology of bacterial biofilms: from structure and rheology to developmental dynamics and environmental adaptation
abstract: Abstract Bacterial biofilms represent a dominant mode of microbial life with profound implications for healthcare, industry, and environmental systems. The mechanical properties of biofilms fundamentally govern their structural development, functional performance, and resilience to external stresses. This review presents a comprehensive multiscale framework integrating experimental techniques and computational modeling to elucidate how mechanics drive biofilm architecture and evolution. We examine the mechanistic basis of initial bacterial attachment, growth-induced mechanical instabilities underlying morphogenesis, and hydrodynamic forces controlling detachment dynamics. Advanced characterization methods spanning atomic force microscopy, microfluidic platforms, and microrheology reveal pronounced mechanical heterogeneity arising from spatially variable extracellular matrix composition and cellular organization. Agent-based models and continuum simulations demonstrate how environmental factors, including nutrient gradients, mechanical stress, and physicochemical conditions, modulate both bulk viscoelastic behavior and local mechanical properties. By synthesizing mechanobiological principles across molecular, cellular, and macroscopic scales, this review establishes a foundation for systematic analysis of biofilm mechanics and highlights critical directions for developing predictive multiscale frameworks that integrate biochemical regulation with mechanical responses.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Bacteria are widespread in both terrestrial and marine environments 1 . When conditions are favorable, they readily attach to surfaces and develop into biofilms, initiating a sequence of morphological and behavioral changes that exert profound effects across clinical, environmental, and industrial systems 1 ,  2 – 3 . These versatile structures, whose impacts can be advantageous or harmful depending on context, have fueled a sustained interest in strategies to regulate biofilm performance for specific environmental demands. Addressing this challenge requires not only understanding the complexity and dynamic nature of biofilms as cellular and polymeric assemblies, but also overcoming the notable difficulties inherent in their comprehensive characterization 4 . Traditionally, the focus of biofilm research centered on biochemical features; however, the recent convergence of advanced experimental methodologies and high-performance computational approaches has enabled the systematic investigation of their mechanical behavior, revealing its pivotal role in biofilm function and resilience 5 ,  6 – 7 . In light of these discoveries, current research increasingly explores ways to decipher and harness the mechanical properties of biofilms, aiming to guide their growth, detachment, and architectural organization with the ultimate goal of engineering functional biofilms tailored for targeted applications 8 , 9 .

Despite notable progress in recent years, the mechanical analysis of biofilms remains a significant challenge and lacks a well-established research framework. As living materials, biofilms continuously undergo morphological evolution, and their mechanical properties are highly dynamic, reflecting the complex interplay of biological processes over time and space. Pronounced heterogeneity further complicates their analysis; biofilms exhibit marked variability in both spatial and temporal dimensions, leading to considerable differences even among samples of the same microbial species. Bulk mechanical behavior has, to some extent, been rationalized in terms of global structure and components, treating biofilms as composite materials, yet a detailed understanding of their internal heterogeneity and its integration into systematic analysis remains an open frontier in the field 6 . Moreover, the inherently complex nature of biofilms means that their mechanical responses are governed not only by internal architecture but also by a constellation of external biochemical factors, many of which differ substantially between species 10 . Structural and mechanical changes frequently originate at the molecular level, where biochemical cues such as nutrient availability or chemical signaling modulate cellular metabolism and intercellular relationships, ultimately shaping the global morphology and performance of the biofilm 11 . Nonetheless, a unified understanding of the underlying mechanisms and their consistency across diverse microbial species is still elusive 12 . To address these challenges, this review systematically assesses the mechanical behavior of biofilms throughout their developmental stages, reviews multiscale methodologies for mechanical characterization, and discusses the biochemical and physical factors that influence these processes, thereby advancing constructive insights toward an integrated and accurate framework for biofilm research.

This review first explores the dynamic interplay of internal stresses and external loads, which drive the morphological evolution of biofilms across distinct developmental stages. This process is marked by sequential transitions from initial surface attachment, through maturation, to eventual dispersal (Fig.  1 ). Building on this foundation, the review then systematically examines both experimental and computational methods currently employed to characterize the global and local mechanical properties and structural features of biofilms, addressing their respective capabilities alongside inherent limitations. Moving deeper, subsequent sections analyze the contributions of intrinsic structural components to biofilm mechanics, while also considering how the surrounding physicochemical and mechanical environments, encompassing both internal and external factors, regulate biofilm behavior, either directly through molecular cues or indirectly via environmental modulation. Finally, drawing together these multifaceted insights, the review outlines prominent research needs and emerging future directions, aiming to foster a more integrated and predictive framework for the study of biofilm mechanics. Fig. 1 Mechanical behavior drives biofilm development throughout its life cycle. The architecture and evolution at each developmental stage, from initial attachment to detachment and dispersal, can be interpreted through the corresponding governing mechanical theory.

sections.heading: Mechanobiology of biofilm development
paragraphs: The development of biofilms typically unfolds through five distinct stages: (i) reversible attachment of cells to a preconditioned surface, (ii) irreversible adhesion, (iii) formation of early three-dimensional architecture, (iv) biofilm maturation, and (v) dispersal of cells into the surrounding environment 13 , 14 . Throughout these stages, individual microbial cells progressively organize into a structured matrix, imparting biofilms with characteristic morphologies at each developmental phase. This dynamic process is fundamentally governed by the interplay between the biofilm’s intrinsic biomechanical properties and its coupled interactions with the external environment, with the nature and magnitude of active and passive mechanical forces shifting in a stage-specific manner to shape biofilm architecture and development 15 ,  16 – 17 . In this section, the discussion centres on how mechanical forces at different scales direct transitions in biofilm structure throughout its development, while elucidating the modulatory role of the biochemical environment in orchestrating this complex mechanobiological process.

sections.heading: Initial bacterial attachment
paragraphs: Initial bacterial attachment to surfaces commonly occurs in environments characterized by fluid shear, both in natural habitats and engineered systems. The fate of a bacterium approaching a surface results from the balance between adhesive forces and hydrodynamic shear: when adhesive interactions are weak, attachment is typically reversible, allowing cells to associate transiently, being removed by shear or Brownian motion. Conversely, when adhesive forces counteract shear, attachment becomes irreversible, paving the way for sustained colonization and biofilm formation. Transition to irreversible attachment coincides with a reduction in flagella reversal rates, reduction in flagella gene expression and the production of biofilm matrix components 13 . In particular, the secretion of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) is essential for the formation of biofilms with an embedding matrix 18 . EPS is composed primarily of exopolysaccharides, proteins, lipids, and extracellular DNA (eDNA), which maintains biofilm integrity and governs its mechanical behaviors 17 . The irreversible transition is often facilitated by polysaccharides, which mediate adhesion between cells and surfaces, thereby dramatically increasing adhesion strength and promoting irreversible association 8 , 19 ,  20 – 21 .

By plotting the energy profile of XDLVO (Fig.  2a ), the primary and secondary energy minima can be found. Although it remains unclear whether the deeper primary energy minimum is associated with bacterial irreversible attachment, several studies have demonstrated that the secondary minimum in the XDLVO model can be used to investigate bacterial initial attachment. For example, Wang, H et al. showed that XDLVO calculations could account for differences in the attachment of various bacterial species to hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces by evaluating the interaction energy at the secondary minimum, the energy barrier between primary and secondary minima, and the predicted maximum repulsive XDLVO force around the second minimum 28 , 30 . Similarly, Feng, G et al. investigated bacterial attachment on anodic alumina surfaces with varying nanopore diameters using confocal and electron microscopy, finding a strong inverse correlation between the maximum predicted repulsive force and the number of attached cells, as predicted by XDLVO theory 31 . Additionally, XDLVO theory has been effectively applied to explain the controlling forces on microbial attachment under the influences of the ionic strength 32 . Studies on  Sphingomonas  sp. GY2B demonstrated that at low ionic strength ( ≤ 20 mM), adhesion onto montmorillonite was primarily governed by long-range electrostatic repulsion, whereas at higher ionic strengths (50–100 mM), short-range van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions became dominant 28 . Collectively, these findings underscore the value of XDLVO theory in quantitatively elucidating how surface properties and solution chemistry govern microbial adhesion under diverse environmental conditions.

In addition, studies have found that more complex factors influence bacterial initial attachment, which are not captured by the XDLVO theory. A central assumption of XDLVO theory is that bacterial cells are idealized as undeformable, perfect spheres 28 . However, recent studies have revealed that bacterial cell shape, elasticity, and the presence of surface pili, hair-like appendages that promote adhesion and mobility, are critical determinants of the attachment process. For instance, surfaces patterned at the nanoscale have been shown to inhibit the adhesion of rod-like  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  and  Escherichia coli  more than that of spherical  Staphylococcus aureus 33 . This difference may be partly explained by the higher turgor pressure associated with the spherical shape of  S. aureus , and, on the other hand, reflects differences in motility, as  S. aureus  lacks flagella, whereas  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  and  E. coli  possess both pili and flagella 33 , 34 . In addition, tuning nanoscale surface patterning has been demonstrated to inhibit the attachment of  S. aureus , and this technique can be used as a strategy to remove biofilms without relying on antibiotics 35 . Duvernoy, M. et al. demonstrated that, in rod-shaped bacteria, the heterogeneous distribution of cell-surface adhesins leads to asymmetric polar adhesive forces at the cell-surface interface, which governs cellular rearrangements during early stages of bacterial attachment 36 . In addition, Gram-negative  Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans  has been observed to use the shape-changing strategy to promote adhesion and subsequent biofilm formation (Fig.  2c ) 37 . The presence of pili on rod-shaped bacteria can alter attachment dynamics: higher shear forces may enhance  P. aeruginosa  adhesion by promoting pilus-driven cell tilting (Fig.  2b ) 38 . In addition to the physical adsorption, bacterial-surface attachment involves more active biological sensing and regulatory processes. Extensive studies, particularly in  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , have demonstrated that bacteria can sense surface contact through mechanosensitive appendages such as flagella and type IV pili, which trigger intracellular signaling cascades involving cyclic AMP (cAMP) and cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP) 39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 . These pathways regulate the attachment by modulating motility, adhesin production, and EPS synthesis. Collectively, multiple interconnected pathways, including mechanosensing, stress response systems, and quorum sensing, coordinate bacterial adaptation to surface-associated lifestyles. Overall, these findings underscore that, at the single-cell level, the structural asymmetry of bacteria and their adaptive responses to substrate and hydrodynamic forces play a defining role in attachment, highlighting the necessity for advanced experimental and computational models that accurately capture these complexities.

sections.heading: Biofilm maturation
paragraphs: Biofilm development begins when surface-attached single cells grow, divide, and an EPS matrix forms, initiating the transition from flat monolayers to three-dimensional structures. The emergent architecture of biofilms is central to their function, driving antimicrobial tolerance in clinical contexts and self-healing survival strategies in environmental and industrial settings. The global organization of a biofilm is predominantly shaped by internal and interfacial stresses, with further modulation by external mechanical conditions.

sections.heading: Global morphogenesis
paragraphs: The mechanical instability and structure development have mutual impacts on each other: 3D surface topography that arises owing to mechanical instabilities caused by biofilm expansion feeds back to slow down expansion and drive contour evolution. Large folds localize most of the bending energy of the system in small regions of large curvature, relaxing the rest of the surface stress 46 . As the biofilm expands further, small parts of it detach from the substrate to form blisters, which are controlled by interfacial energy. Biofilm on stiffer agar with lower normalized adhesive energy tends to form regularly and closely spaced blisters, resulting in a nearly circular biofilm shape. This is because the emergence of a blister creates an extra dimension into which newly produced biomass can be distributed and thereby slows down the expansion 44 .

Such morphological features may provide survival advantages for biofilms. Cells in blisters are less susceptible to the lethal effects of antibiotics that diffuse in from the substrate than are cells residing in the base of the biofilm, presumably because cells in blisters are located further away from the antibiotic source 44 . In addition, it is hypothesized that internal stresses may serve as a sophisticated self-repair mechanism: upon physical damage, the release of stored internal stress can trigger local expansion, promoting recovery in the affected region. For instance, the self-healing ability of  B. subtilis  biofilm depends on its age and wrinkle morphology 49 .

When biofilms form at solid–liquid interfaces, nutrient gradients and hydrodynamic conditions in the fluid environment come into play. As bacterial biomass accumulates, biofilms develop into distinct clusters or hemispherical structures, with the developmental stage often quantified by the number of constituent cells ( N ) 50 . Early-stage biofilms containing fewer than 100 cells typically exist as two-dimensional monolayers, while biofilms of intermediate size (200–3000 cells) display hemispherical symmetry under low-shear conditions and adopt droplet-like morphologies in high-shear environments 50 . At the mesoscale, the upper regions tend to be more porous, whereas the bottom regions are denser and exhibit different distributions of components 51 ,  52 – 53 . Fluid-induced pressure and vibration can gradually consolidate biofilms, leading to increased density over time 51 , 52 , 54 . This effect is more pronounced in the bottom layers due to longer growth duration and accumulation of inert biomass, resulting in higher composite density near the substratum 51 , 54 .

sections.heading: Cellular arrangement of rod-shaped bacteria
paragraphs: For rod-shaped bacteria with poles (as in  E. coli, V. cholerae, P. aeruginosa ), cells within biofilm often display active nematic order during their developing process 50 , 55 ,  56 – 57 . Such active nematic order emerges via an initial one-dimensional bundled growth, followed by two-dimensional in-plane expansion into patterns with local nematic order. Subsequently, cells undergo verticalization, forming a three-dimensional convex architecture. Despite substantial differences in extracellular matrix composition and cellular properties across species, biofilm architecture is predominantly shaped by shared biophysical mechanisms, particularly internal and interfacial stresses and further modulated by external mechanical conditions 6 , 58 , 59 .

First, adjacent rod-shaped bacterial cells interact through the competition between growth-induced active forces and passive steric interactions. While active growth tends to disorder the system, steric forces promote the formation of closely packed nematic structures. As a result, dense rod-shaped bacterial cells growing on a frictional substrate plane exhibit nematic microdomains with uniform characteristic length (Fig.  3b ) 60 , 61 . Since both active and passive forces are proportional to the cell density, the size of the microdomain is almost uniform across the biofilm despite the higher density of bacterial cells at the center 61 .

EPSs, as major structural components of the biofilm matrix, drive biofilm structural organization through bridging interactions or depletion attraction. Bridging occurs when the polymers have an attractive interaction to the cell surface, allowing them to simultaneously adsorb onto multiple cells while bringing these cells into proximity 62 . Depletion, on the other hand, is driven by entropy and takes place when non-attractive or repulsive polymers and cells coexist 62 . Bridging aggregation is induced by crosslinks between different EPS types mediated by accessory proteins, typically resulting in loose and disordered aggregates (Fig.  3c ) 63 . Depletion aggregates arise from the reduction of excluded volume for the depletants as large bacterial cells approach one another, and thereby leads to a parallel, space-filling cellular arrangement (Fig.  3c ) 63 . From the survival perspective, depletion aggregation contributes to antibiotic tolerance by inducing SulA-dependent growth arrest 64 .

Chemical and biological environmental factors further regulate aggregation behavior. Nutrient availability-related EPS secretion is highly involved in this aggregation process. In  Vibrio cholerae  biofilm, as the coverage of VPS on the bacterial cell surface decreases, the biofilm system converts from bridging aggregation to depletion aggregation 65 . A higher EPS-to-cell density ratio is likewise associated with enhanced phase separation, and similar mechanisms have been reported in  P. aeruginosa  and  E. coli  biofilms 63 , 65 . In addition to biofilm-produced EPS, host polymers present in the surrounding environment can also induce depletion aggregation 64 . Meanwhile, osmotic pressure arising from the exclusion of polymer particles between two adjacent bacterial cells in the polymer solution induces the intercellular attraction and forms a cable pattern 63 , 64 , 66 .

Following 2D expansion, rod-shaped bacteria experience a verticalization process to enter the 3D growth stage. In the initial attachment stage, founder cells secrete adhesin and form a bonded layer that persists in the mature biofilm and drives the reorientation of cells as cell density increases 56 , 67 . As the local surface pressure overcomes the cell-surface adhesion, which favors horizontal orientation, the cell verticalization begins (Fig.  3d ). This local mechanical instability varies with cell length and division 68 . As shorter cells prefer to verticalize due to surface compression, longer cells can be buckled up by out-of-plane torque 68 . The differential oriented growth brought by the verticalization of cells in the center area drives the motion of cells, resulting in the spreading out of the verticalization area and radial arrangement of the surrounding cells 69 . At the frontier of biofilm expansion, outermost cells tend to align tangentially to the radial direction, which arises from the torque balance 60 , 70 . Later, central cells migrate into the upper layer, forming a multilayer structure with reduced radius from bottom to top 70 .

The aspect ratio of the resulting convex biofilm structure is jointly determined by cell shape, cellular mechanical interactions, and friction between the biofilm and the substrate. Reorientation events not only increase the cell density at the center of the biofilm, but also lead to a faster biofilm expansion rate in height than in radius 56 . In general, shorter cells have a higher probability of reorientation, whereas longer cells yield more rapidly expanding, flatter biofilms 68 . Continuum modeling, by reproducing the biofilm expansion velocity field, further suggests that stronger cell–surface adhesion increases the height-to-radius aspect ratio of biofilms 59 . In addition, computational simulations with agent-based models (ABMs) of biofilms identified cell aspect ratio and cell density as the major contributing factors determining biofilm architectures 71 .

Different EPS work synergistically in the formation of the biofilm 3D structure. Underproduction or overproduction of one of the critical EPSs can inhibit its proper development 56 . Though  V. cholerae  cells lacking VPS secretion can still stick to surfaces, subsequently produced cells fail to form a cohesive biofilm matrix and are therefore not retained, but instead are lost to the surrounding medium, as existing RbmA, RbmC, and Bap1 are not able to accumulate on the cell surface 67 , 72 , 73 . Also, introduction of the Rg mutation into the RbmA-lacking strain drastically elevated expression of rbmC, bap1, and vpsL 59 . On the other hand, the overexpression of Bap1 leads to enhanced attachment of cells to the surface, which impedes the transition into the third dimension 56 .

sections.heading: Mechanical environment regulation
paragraphs: As rod-shaped bacteria biofilms behave like active nematics with self-generated stresses, they can regulate their boundaries as their boundary conditions change due to spatial confinement 74 . During the 2D expansion stage, biofilms initiated from circularly distributed cells and growing inward develop a radial cell arrangement, in contrast to unconfined expansion colonies, which exhibit microdomains with random local orientations 75 . This radial ordering arises because the circular confinement, set by a critical radius, dictates the growth-induced velocity profiles, which in turn stabilize radial bacterial orientation 75 .

Biofilms growing under hydrogel confinement provide a representative example of mechanically regulated morphogenesis. Their global morphology and internal cellular organization are jointly governed by cell–surface friction, gel elasticity, and surface adhesion 74 , 76 . When confined by soft hydrogels, the biofilm approaches a spherical morphology, whereas in stiffer gels it evolves from a prolate to spherical, then to an oblate shape eventually 77 . At the single-cell level, the biofilm develops a well-defined bipolar nematic ordering: rod-shaped cells near the biofilm-gel interface progressively align radially around the two poles, with ordering initiating at the interface and propagating inward (Fig.  3e ) 76 . This orientational ordering originates from growth-generated stress anisotropy 74 . As proliferation pushes against the surrounding gel, tensile stresses arise in the gel and define the principal stress directions 76 , 77 . In turn, the stresses in gels are transmitted back to the cells through EPS mediation, aligning cells along the direction of maximum tensile stress 76 , 77 . EPS, therefore, becomes necessary in biofilm-gel mechanical interaction. The increase in cell ordering is tightly coupled to the global morphological transition 77 . A continuum solid model considering the biofilm as a growing inclusion within an elastic medium shows that the stiffness contrast between the biofilm and the hydrogel determines morphology via mechanical energy accumulation 74 , 77 . When growth drives the gel beyond its elastic limit, damage relaxes the stress field and triggers a morphological transition 77 .

sections.heading: Biofilm detachment and dispersal
paragraphs: During the late maturation stage of biofilm development, bacterial cells egress from the biofilm to resume a planktonic lifestyle by spontaneous cell dispersion or detachment due to external physical forces, which alters the structural integrity and spatial organization of the community 79 . Biofilm shedding can occur in multiple forms, including individual surface-associated cells, flocs, or large EPS-embedded clusters, thereby exerting distinct impacts on biofilm morphology 80 ,  81 ,  82 – 83 .

To address the challenge of removing detrimental biofilms in various industrial contexts, such as on medical instruments, food processing equipment, and in industrial water systems, the role of mechanical forces in biofilm detachment has been extensively studied. This is because many biocides can be toxic to non-target organisms and pose environmental pollution risks 84 ,  85 – 86 . In these studies, hydrodynamic conditions have become a primary focus, not only because they create environments that favor biofilm development and propagation, but also due to their direct relevance across numerous practical applications.

Shear and tensile forces imposed by fluid flow can directly cause biofilm detachment. Surface erosion refers to the continuous loss of small particles ( < 20 μm), rendering the biofilm surface smoother, while sloughing means large biomass clusters (50–500 μm) detach episodically and increase the biofilm surface roughness (defined here as the root-mean-square deviation of surface height) 87 . Flow-induced detachment can be a combination of erosion and sloughing events. The impacts of fluid field on the detachment dynamically couple with biofilm heterogeneous mechanical properties and its morphology 88 . A rough biofilm surface increases the spatial heterogeneity of shear stresses and generates localized amplification at protruding regions above the mean biofilm thickness 80 , 89 . In this context, biofilm roughness can be evaluated based on its influence on the local flow field velocity profiles to re-establishment 90 . When cell clusters are sufficiently dispersed, the flow can re-establish so that each cluster experiences a similar shear force 90 . In contrast, rougher biofilms typically exhibit more spatially variable detachment patterns, whereas smoother biofilms tend to shed smaller fragments more continuously 90 . Although rough biofilms may exhibit reduced detachment of surface-associated cells due to localized low-shear regions, their structural heterogeneity can promote stress concentration and increase susceptibility to large-scale sloughing. Thus, biofilm roughness exerts scale-dependent effects on detachment dynamics 90 , 91 .

Growth rate influences the behaviors of biofilms under fluid forces by modulating their structural organization. High growth rates trigger instability in biofilm accumulation, making it easier to detach than biofilms with low growth rates under similar hydrodynamic conditions and biofilm strength 89 . From a mechanical perspective, detachment is initiated when local cohesive failure occurs within the EPS matrix as interfacial shear stress surpasses the biofilm’s cohesive yield strength 79 , 92 . Picioreanu et al. applied local distortion-energy theory to study how specific modes of shedding affect the surface roughness in 2D continuum biofilm growth models 89 . The significant influence of EPS amount on the mechanical properties of biofilms and biofilm detachment has been studied in a 3D ABM framework 93 . However, hydrodynamic conditions influence not only biofilm structure but also their material properties (as discussed further in the next section), making the prediction of biofilm detachment behavior through modeling more challenging 94 .

Over time, the emergence of cavities promoted by low dissolved-oxygen (DO) concentrations within the deeper regions of long-aged biofilm deteriorates its adhesive and tensile strength 90 . Once the shear forces exceed the adhesion strength of the biofilm-substratum interface, the internal adhesion of the biofilm matrix still holds the biofilm together, thus causing the entire biofilm to be sheared off 95 . Unified multiple-component cellular automaton simulations suggest that low DO concentrations promote cavity formation in the basal layers of biofilms, leading to structural weakening and reduced adhesion and tensile strength in long-aged biofilms 54 . Consistently, experimental observation shows the progressive loss of adhesion strength during biofilm ageing, particularly in deeper regions 95 .

In addition to passive detachment mechanisms, biofilms can also undergo active dispersal processes regulated by cellular activities, in which EPS components and cell surface properties are modulated in response to nutrient limitation. As mentioned in Section “ Cellular Arrangement of Rod-Shaped Bacteria ”, nutrient consumption reduces VPS coverage on  V. cholerae  cell surfaces and promotes the transition from bridging to depletion aggregates 65 . RbmB enzyme activity further accelerates this process through VPS degradation, producing depletion aggregates that are more susceptible to flow-induced removal 65 , 96 . Similarly, reduced carbon and nitrogen availability leads  M. smegmatis  aggregates to disperse, even in the absence of external flow 97 . Regardless of the signal transduction mechanism, a surface adhesin must mediate the aggregation phenotype 97 . From a mechanical perspective, such dispersal processes can be interpreted as the changes of biofilm cohesiveness mediated by weakened intercellular or cell-matrix interaction. Evidence suggests that mycobacteria can dynamically regulate cell envelope composition and surface hydrophobicity, which may represent a potential regulatory mechanism underlying C/N-controlled aggregation and dispersal responses through modifications of intercellular interactions 97 ,  98 – 99 .

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The importance of physical dynamics in biofilm development has been highlighted by numerous controlled-variable studies. Nevertheless, biofilm development is intrinsically a multiphysics process involving strong coupling between mechanical, biological, and biochemical factors. Mechanical processes not only shape biofilm architecture and influence survival-related functions such as antibiotic tolerance, but also operate in close coupling with biological regulation. In turn, biological and biochemical factors modulate these mechanical processes, highlighting the reciprocal interplay between physical dynamics and biological function.

A representative example that spans almost all stages of biofilm development is quorum sensing (QS). Once a critical population density is reached, QS-mediated gene regulation can alter bacterial behavior through the production, release, and group-wide detection of signal molecules called autoinducers and thereby influence the recolonization and dispersal of the bacteria group. In many species, QS controls the production of protein enzyme or EPSs to exert impacts on biofilm formation and robustness 100 ,  101 ,  102 – 103 . The impacts of QS on bacteria colonies are highly complex, which not only reciprocally influence biofilm formation but also vary with environmental context 104 , 105 . Previous studies (e.g., Nadell et al.) have extensively discussed the roles of collective behaviors, including QS, in shaping biofilm development and architecture 84 . Nevertheless, how such biologically regulated processes can be systematically incorporated into physically grounded models of biofilm developmental dynamics remains an open challenge. As discussed throughout this review, biofilm development involves a transition from single cells to multicellular composite systems. The theory of collective behavior also suggests that apparently coordinated aggregates can emerge from the local interactions of individual cells following relatively simple behavioral rules 84 . Establishing multiscale integrative frameworks that couple physical dynamics with biological regulation will therefore be essential for understanding the active behaviors of biofilms.

Owing to this complexity, modeling studies are particularly valuable for elucidating the underlying mechanisms of biofilm development, even though their predictive capability may remain limited. As discussed above, biofilm morphogenesis is driven by cellular-scale dynamics and emerges from the coupling of biological, chemical, and mechanical processes across spatially heterogeneous microenvironments. Widely used continuum models typically consider biofilm as an active continuum with homogeneous mechanical properties. By incorporating growth-induced active stresses, expansion dynamics and nutrient diffusion, such models enable the prediction of internal stress distributions and morphological evolution under different mechanical conditions.

Another modeling framework that provides a cell-resolved description is ABM. ABMs represent individual bacterial cells as idealized geometric objects, typically spheres or rods, and are endowed with biophysical processes, such as growth, division, secretion and death, which can be further coupled to nutrient consumption and transport described by continuum reaction–diffusion fields 6 , 106 ,  107 ,  108 – 109 . Meanwhile, the EPSs are often represented implicitly as a soft shell encapsulating bacterial cells with viscous drag, or explicitly as a simplified discrete spherical body contributing to inter-particle interactions, or simplified as a continuum field incorporated into the viscous environment 71 , 110 ,  111 – 112 . These particles interact through prescribed interaction potentials including steric repulsion, adhesion and friction, and are subject to mechanical interactions with the substrate and spatial confinement. The particle's motion can also be coupled with a fluid field to capture the biofilm structure evolution and detachment 78 , 112 . Some ABMs also incorporate stochastic cellular processes, such as localized cell death or phenotypic variability, to capture the role of probabilistic events in biofilm structural development 47 , 113 . Within this framework, complex biofilm architectures can emerge from local mechanical interactions and growth rules, providing an important physical basis for understanding biofilm morphogenesis.

However, a unified multiscale theoretical framework for biofilm mechanics remains underdeveloped. In addition to the difficulty of quantitatively incorporating biological regulatory processes into mechanical models, a gap also exists between microscale ABMs and continuum descriptions. Microscale ABMs have yet to fully capture the continuously produced EPS gel matrix that encapsulates bacterial cells, and the mechanical and physical parameters employed in these models remain weakly grounded in experimental mechanical characterization 50 , 56 , 63 , 114 . In most ABMs, biofilms are described as collections of discrete particles whose interactions are governed by prescribed mechanical laws, typically including short-range repulsive forces, adhesion-mediated attractive forces, and frictional or viscous interactions 68 , 69 , 74 , 115 , 116 . These interaction laws are commonly formulated based on geometric descriptors such as interparticle distance, overlap, or contact area, and the associated parameters are often indirectly estimated from experimentally measurable quantities such as cell–cell or cell–substrate separation distances 68 , 71 , 117 ,  118 ,  119 – 120 .

Some studies further incorporate damping terms or viscoelastic contact formulations to account for energy dissipation during cell interactions, while others introduce more detailed descriptions, such as explicit adhesive bonds or heterogeneous interaction sites, to better represent EPS-mediated interactions 65 , 121 ,  122 – 123 . Nevertheless, many interaction models in ABMs are often formulated in a phenomenological manner, and the parameters used across different models lack clear biophysical interpretation, which constrains the modeling of biofilm evolution across different stages of the biofilm lifecycle. Recent experimental advances, such as atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurements of cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesion forces, provide quantitative mechanical parameters that could help establish more physically grounded interaction models 124 . Integrating such experimentally measured mechanical properties into modeling frameworks, therefore, remains an important direction for improving the physical realism of biofilm simulations and extending their applicability to broader biological and engineering contexts.

sections.heading: Bulk mechanical properties
paragraphs: The mechanical stability of biofilms is intrinsically linked to their physiological functioning and to their utility in biotechnological applications 4 . Biofilms can be considered soft matter systems composed of cells embedded in a hydrated cross-linked polymer matrix, where cells act similarly to colloidal particles and the surrounding EPS matrix mimics a cross-linked polymer gel 17 . This framework draws useful parallels with soft matter physics and supports the prevailing view of biofilms as viscoelastic materials 17 . Mechanical parameters commonly measured in deformation analyses include apparent Young’s modulus, shear modulus, storage modulus, and loss modulus (Table  1 ). To assess biofilm stability and failure mechanisms, key indicators such as yield strength, as well as cohesive and adhesive strength, are directly or indirectly measured (Table  1 ). In addition to their viscoelastic mechanical response, biofilms permit fluid transport through the hydrated EPS matrix. Under mechanical loading, matrix deformation can drive pore-fluid redistribution or drainage, introducing a poroelastic contribution to the apparent mechanical response. Thereby, the global physicochemical behavior of biofilms is often described using parameters commonly applied to porous materials, including permeability, hydraulic resistance, and effective porosity. In such hydrated porous systems, the measured mechanical behavior and the time required to reach mechanical equilibrium may also depend on the characteristic size of the biofilm, reflecting the time needed for fluid to redistribute through the porous matrix. sections.heading: Bulk mechanical characterization
paragraphs: Biofilm grown on solid–air interface can be tested by uniaxial compression test and rheometers. Biofilm samples are either scraped from their native growth surfaces and transferred to a rheometer or grown directly on rheometer plates for in situ measurements. Although scraping may disrupt structural integrity, it offers greater flexibility in controlling growth conditions. Despite the inherent roughness of biofilm samples, bulk mechanical analyses typically employ averaged dimensions (e.g., height or thickness) in deformation analysis. The apparent Young’s modulus and yield strength of unsaturated  P. aeruginosa  were measured by uniaxial compression test, in which the compressive Young’s modulus was found to be consistent with weak polymer gels 125 , 126 . Biofilm viscoelasticity is typically characterized with rheometers through creep and oscillatory shear protocols. Within the small-deformation regime, measurements across different stress levels and oscillation frequencies provide key parameters of linear viscoelasticity 127 ,  128 – 129 . Beyond the linear viscoelastic regime, large-amplitude oscillatory shear (LAOS) exposes pronounced nonlinear responses 130 , 131 . At elevated strain amplitudes, secondary loops and stress asymmetry indicate structural rearrangement and partial breakdown of the biofilm matrix, with species-specific tendencies toward intracycle shear thinning or thickening 131 . Further rheological analyses focusing on mechanical robustness demonstrate that biofilms can endure large deformations and recover stiffness after yielding, underscoring the strong elastic resilience of the polymeric matrix 132 . In failure tests, characterizing the force–distance curves and the amount of biological material transferred between the two contacting surfaces enables rheometric measurements to differentiate between adhesive and cohesive failure of biofilm samples 133 . In addition, adhesive strength can be quantified using capillary peeling methods, which measure the minimum effective mechanical energy per unit area required to detach the biofilm from a hydrophilic surface at a constant peeling angle 134 .

For biofilms developing at solid–liquid interfaces, mechanical loading can be applied via controlled shear flow, where the imposed flow velocity is translated into hydrodynamic drag or wall shear stress through fluid mechanical theory 135 , 136 . Shear flow experiments in flow cells established stress–strain relationships by correlating calculated wall shear stress, derived from flow velocity, with the measured elongation of individual biofilm clusters 137 . The results revealed a time-dependent mechanical response: at low shear or under short-duration disturbances, biofilms exhibited predominantly elastic behavior with minimal hysteresis, whereas at higher shear or over longer timescales, typical viscous behavior including hysteresis, residual strain, and creep were observed 137 . The tensile strength and failure strain of biofilms grown in microfluidic chips under creeping flow were determined using time-resolved microscopy combined with Stokes flow theory 93 . The internal tensile stress was thereby calculated by integrating the distributed hydrodynamic drag force and normalizing by the average cross-sectional area 93 .

Such non-conventional mechanical testing approaches can also characterize deformation by capturing structural changes using confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) or optical coherence tomography (OCT), combined with parameter identification through finite-element modeling (FEM) based on linear elastic or poroelastic constitutive models. A microfluidic study employs air pressure to control the stress applied to a flexible PDMS membrane, in which membrane deformation is captured by CLSM and a linear elastic constitutive model is used in FEM 138 . Similarly, Young’s modulus of biofilms grown under solid–liquid conditions has been quantified by combining OCT-based geometric reconstruction with fluid–structure coupled poroelastic modeling 139 .

Factors that may contribute to variations in mechanical behavior, such as bacterial strains and cultivation conditions, are listed where available. When data are derived from studies involving mutants or specific treatments, only the untreated control data are reported here for consistency.

Where mechanical parameters were obtained from deformation fitting, the corresponding constitutive models are noted. However, due to the lack of standardized testing protocols in biofilm mechanics, readers are encouraged to consult the original references for detailed experimental procedures and parameter calculation methods.

sections.heading: Bulk mechanical impact factors
paragraphs: Different extracellular matrix components make distinct contributions to the viscoelastic mechanical properties of biofilms. Mutant strains with altered EPS expression or enzymatic treatments are often used to identify the mechanical roles of individual matrix components. For example, rheological measurements of  E. coli  biofilms with genetically modified production of curli fibers, colanic acid and poly-β-1,6-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (PGA) showed that curli amyloid fibers dominate the mechanical response of the matrix 128 . Strains expressing curli exhibited significantly higher storage modulus and cohesive energy, indicating a stronger and more elastic matrix network, whereas mutants lacking curli fibers displayed markedly reduced viscoelasticity 128 . In contrast, variations in colanic acid and PGA production had comparatively weaker effects on the bulk mechanical response 128 . Enzymatic treatments such as DNase and proteases markedly alter biofilm viscoelasticity by selectively degrading key structural components of the EPS matrix 140 . DNase cleaves extracellular DNA (eDNA), which contributes to biofilm mechanical integrity by forming structural networks that bridge cells within the matrix 140 . In contrast, proteases degrade extracellular matrix proteins that act as adhesive and cross-linking elements, stabilizing interactions between cells and polysaccharides. The removal of these structural polymers disrupts the connectivity of the EPS network, leading to reduced elastic modulus and viscosity and rendering the mucus-like biofilm matrix more deformable 129 .

The viscoelasticity of biofilms may undergo extensive temporal changes during biofilm development as the composition and relative abundance of EPS components evolve. For example, mucoid variants of  P. aeruginosa , which overproduce alginate, and RSCVs that overproduce P sl  (Polysaccharide synthesis locus) and Pel (Pellicle polysaccharide), exhibit distinct temporal trends in their viscoelastic properties compared with wild type (WT) biofilms 125 . While WT biofilms display fluctuating viscoelastic behavior during maturation, RSCV and mucoid biofilms progressively transition toward more elastic-solid-like behavior, likely reflecting the stabilization and densification of the EPS polymer network over time 125 .

Water content is another major determinant of creep behavior, constituting ~98% by mass of EPS 141 . Biofilm in dry and fully hydrated states has different relaxation times and Young’s modulus. Increasing soluble EPS production increases the potential for bound water content and biofilm osmotic potentials 141 , 142 . Through the entire hydration process, the Young’s modulus of the biofilm continuously decreases with increasing volume 20 . Stress relaxation may involve a number of processes, like the outflow of water and EPS from the biofilm and re-arrangement of the bacteria in the biofilm 143 . Water has the lowest viscosity in a biofilm; the fastest principal component in the Maxwell modeling for biofilm stress relaxation was associated with the outflow of water and soluble polysaccharides 143 , 144 . The presence of bacteria themselves as the heaviest masses is included in the first principal component, with an inverse impact of bacterial prevalence with respect to the presence of water and the free space in a biofilm available for bacterial re-arrangement processes 144 . An intermediate component was related to other EPSs, while a distinguishable role was assigned to intact eDNA, which modulates its interaction with other matrix constituents to control its contribution to viscoelastic relaxation under mechanical stress 140 .

To characterize biofilm poroelastic behavior, Jafari et al. combined in situ optical coherence tomography with a fluid–structure interaction model to examine biofilm deformation during compression 145 . Treating the biofilm as a deformable porous medium in which fluid transport follows Darcy’s law, the authors quantified effective porosity and permeability from the measured compression dynamics 145 . The results showed that compression-induced pore closure reduces porosity and permeability, thereby increasing hydraulic resistance and modifying the mechanical response of the biofilm layer. Similarly, studies by Laspidou et al. and Picioreanu et al. demonstrated that large hydrodynamic stresses associated with high Reynolds number flows can induce biofilm deformation that leads to pore closure within the matrix, thereby increasing the effective elastic modulus, a phenomenon referred to as stiffening (hardening) effects 54 , 139 . Bilayer porous medium simulations further show that biofilm hydraulic resistance is strongly controlled by the dense bottom layer 146 . These findings highlight the tight coupling between pore architecture, hydraulic transport and mechanical behavior in biofilms. It is noteworthy that structural and transport metrics such as porosity, permeability, and water content are strongly interdependent in hydrated biofilms, and therefore require coupled analyses to properly interpret their mechanical behavior.

Beyond the direct impact of hydrodynamic forces on pore structure, flow conditions can also influence biofilm mechanical properties through growth history. Biofilms developed under higher shear have been shown to exhibit increased adhesive and cohesive strength 94 , 147 , 148 . Chen et al. reported that biofilms grown under higher flow velocities tend to develop more compact structures, which in turn enhances their adhesive strength 148 . This strengthening may also arise from shear-induced alignment of EPS polymer strands, which promotes intermolecular interactions such as hydrogen bonding and electrostatic attraction within the matrix 94 . At a finer scale, mechanical characterizations have shown that hydrodynamic conditions can significantly influence the mechanical heterogeneity within biofilms, which may serve as an important origin of the observed changes in their macroscopic mechanical behavior 52 . This aspect will be discussed in detail in Section “ Mechanical heterogeneity ”.

For biofilms growing at solid–air interfaces, substratum water availability and nutrient supply are important environmental factors influencing biofilm mechanical properties. As discussed above, the water content of biofilms is one of the determinants. Therefore, substrate water availability influences biofilm stiffness by regulating the hydration of the EPS matrix. Biofilms attached to highly hydrated substrates retain greater water content, resulting in lower stiffness 142 . Nutrient availability modulates the production and molecular organization of the EPS matrix. For example, nutrient limitation can promote the formation and structural ordering of curli amyloid fibers in  E. coli  biofilms, leading to increased matrix cohesion and higher biofilm stiffness 149 . In addition, exposure to divalent and trivalent metal ions can alter the elastic modulus and robustness of biofilms, primarily through specific interactions with EPS components. For example, the addition of 150 mM Fe(III) balances the softening induced by the dilution with water and increases  P. aeruginosa  biofilm elasticity by ~500-fold 132 . At the same time, the metal ions treatment changes the biofilm texture immediately upon mixing, indicating that the impacts of external chemical stimulus probably do not require a metabolic response from the bacteria within the biofilm 132 . Instead, metal ion treatment may directly act on the biofilm polymers or on their interaction with the bacteria 132 . Similar effects were also observed in  E. coli  biofilm 150 . The different responses observed in strains producing curli and cellulose fibers further indicate that the matrix is the determining factor in the effects of metal ions 150 . Interestingly, the same ion can have opposite effects in different bacterial species. While Cu(II) reinforces  B. subtilis B-1  biofilms, it weakens those produced by  P. aeruginosa 132 , 151 . Such complex mechanisms may require understanding at the molecular level 152 .

In summary, the relationship between biofilm bulk mechanical properties and their compositional and morphological features has been investigated extensively. Although biofilms formed by different microbial species display distinct characteristics and behaviors, many influencing factors demonstrate consistent trends across species. Assessing the compositional content and global physical parameters of biofilms often provides a preliminary indication of their mechanical properties. Despite the efficiency of these mechanical characterization approaches, the reported measurements often lack comparability across studies. As summarized in Table  1 , values of commonly used mechanical indicators span a wide range even for similar biofilm systems. This limitation is partly due to the absence of standardized mechanical characterization methods, which makes it difficult to directly compare biofilm properties across different experimental conditions. Therefore, by discussing the mechanical characteristics of biofilms and their governing factors, this review aims to help promote the development of more standardized mechanical characterization frameworks. For instance, as discussed in this section, the mechanical properties of biofilms evolve significantly during their development, suggesting that monitoring time and continuous tracking measurements can be valuable.

Another important aspect from a mechanical perspective lies in data interpretation, particularly the assumptions made during mechanical testing and the definitions of key parameters. For example, rheological measurements of biofilm storage and loss moduli typically assume no relative displacement between the sample and the testing platform. However, in situ grown biofilms, while preserving native structures, may not fully satisfy this assumption. Similarly, uniaxial compression tests may induce fluid drainage during loading, leading to size effects in poroelastic biofilm samples.

sections.heading: Mechanical heterogeneity
paragraphs: Biofilms exhibit pronounced biological and physicochemical heterogeneity, arising from complex and interdependent relationships among their constituent components. Variations in matrix composition, cellular organization, and structural morphology directly lead to heterogeneous mechanical properties, which may manifest as global or local gradients as well as clustered spatial distributions. Consequently, microscale characterization techniques are essential for resolving the mechanical properties of biofilms across length scales ranging from nanometers to micrometers. These approaches enable measurements at the single-cell level or localized measurements that average the mechanical contributions of tens of bacterial cells together with their surrounding EPS matrix.

sections.heading: Mechanical heterogeneity characterization
paragraphs: Microscale experiments not only complement bulk mechanical measurements but also capture spatial mechanical heterogeneity that cannot be resolved by bulk characterization. In situ contact-based deformation analysis, such as nanoprobes, micropipettes, or microcantilevers, provides spatially resolved viscoelastic responses near the biofilm surface 153 ,  154 – 155 . Owing to the viscoelastic nature of biofilms, AFM has been used to construct nanoscale force spectroscopy measurements by probing the biofilm at different loading rates 155 , 156 . This nanoscale test distinguishes the viscoelastic response of bacterial cells and EPS matrix across different timescales and frequencies 156 , 157 . These results indicate that bacterial cells exhibit higher apparent stiffness, which can be three orders of magnitude larger than the EPS 156 , 158 . The EPS matrix behaves as a softer and highly viscoelastic polymer network, displaying stronger frequency-dependent responses and larger loss angles, indicative of greater viscous dissipation (Fig.  4a ) 156 , 158 . Such observations provide microscale evidence, from a polymer-physics perspective, for the decisive role of the EPS matrix in determining biofilm cohesiveness. Besides its widespread use in characterizing biofilms at solid–air interfaces, AFM also enables surface mechanical probing of biofilms grown at solid–liquid interfaces. Unlike bulk viscoelastic properties that depend strongly on flow conditions, the Young’s modulus of the superficial biofilm layer (0–1 μm) correlates more closely with microcolony size and morphology 159 . Another technique that allows probing the local mechanical properties within deeper regions of biofilms is particle-tracking microrheology (PTM), which infers local rheological properties by tracking the motion trajectories of bacteria or embedded tracer particles and analyzing their mean square displacement (MSD) (Fig.  4c ) 76 , 160 . PTM studies on  S. aureus ,  P. aeruginosa , and  E. coli  biofilms grown at solid–liquid interfaces under different flow conditions generally revealed a layered mechanical organization, with a stiffer bottom region and a more compliant surface layer (thickness of the layers ranging from 5 to 20 μm, depending on the overall thickness) 76 , 160 , 161 . Local compliance can vary by up to nearly one order of magnitude between the basal and surface regions, which implies that using a single shear strain threshold as a failure criterion may not accurately describe biofilm detachment (Fig.  4b ) 162 . A confocal Brillouin microscopy (CBM) study further provided mechanical property mapping of biofilms across different depth planes, showing that the mechanical heterogeneity of  P. aeruginosa  biofilms grown under shear flow also exhibits scale-dependent characteristics (Fig.  4d ) 163 . In relatively thinner colonies, stiffness was observed to increase toward the colony center, whereas in thicker biofilms a mechanically stiff outer shell surrounding a softer core, or even a void region, was identified 163 . The results further suggest that the internal mechanical heterogeneity also evolves during biofilm development. In particular, the stiffness contrast between the outer layer and the interior becomes more pronounced as the  P. aeruginosa  biofilm develops from 48 h to 72 h 163 .

sections.heading: Mechanical heterogeneity impact factors
paragraphs: The origins of mechanical heterogeneity in biofilms lie in the spatially uneven distribution of cells and extracellular matrix components. In  S. aureus  biofilms, local compliance variations are highly correlated with the density of bacterial cells (Fig.  4c ) 76 . The authors suggested that regions containing larger numbers of neighboring bacterial cells exhibit higher stiffness, which may be due to enhanced cell-cell adhesion and increased sharing of extracellular matrix components 76 . However, in a study on the compliance gradients within  E. coli  biofilms, Galy et al. proposed that the adhesin expression plays a dominant role in determining both the local average values and spatial distribution of compliance, rather than correlated increase in cell density 161 . Similarly, in  V. cholerae  biofilms, the local distribution of spring modulus in a 3D Delaunay tessellation model correlates with the abundance of VPS, a key determinant of intercellular cohesiveness (Fig.  4e ) 164 . These observations suggest that biofilms behave as composite materials composed of bacterial cells and EPS matrices with distinct mechanical properties. Their local mechanical behavior therefore, reflects the combined contributions of these phases and their interactions. However, although many AFM studies have characterized the mechanical properties of individual bacterial cells, how these local measurements translate into the bulk mechanical behavior of biofilms remains unclear.

EPS production and bacterial growth are tightly linked to biological processes within the biofilm, mainly through the metabolic responses regulated by the surrounding chemical microenvironment 7 . For example, under identical flow conditions,  P. aeruginosa  biofilms grown at lower bulk DO conditions exhibit higher compliance values in the top layer, which can be attributed to the difference in oxygen consumption (Fig.  4b ) 162 . In the top layer exposed to low DO conditions, increases in compliance may be correlated with the less dense structures caused by the low growth rate of cells 162 . Several studies have shown that oxygen gradients within biofilms are primarily determined by biological activity 163 , 164 . Thereby, the properties of the bottom layer of the biofilm are less correlated with the DO in the bulk liquid 159 . Another possible explanation for observed stiffness gradients is that biofilm growth tends to proceed in directions of minimal mechanical resistance, which aligns gradients of stiffness with those of oxygen concentration, nutrient availability, and growth rate 7 , 165 .

The hydrodynamic environment influences not only the macroscopic mechanical properties of biofilms but also their internal mechanical heterogeneity.  P. aeruginosa  and  E. coli  biofilms, which exhibit a compliant layered structure, exhibit similar trends adapting to the flow velocity 161 , 162 . In early stages, biofilms grown under lower flow velocities exhibit a broader distribution of more compliant regions (tested shear stress ranging from 0.2–10 mPa) 161 , 162 . Because the applied shear stresses were far below the cohesive strength of the biofilm, deformation induced directly by shear forces alone is insufficient to explain the observed structural changes 161 . Such mechanical remodeling under low shear conditions is more likely to result from biological adaptation rather than purely passive mechanical responses 161 . A transcriptomic analysis of  E. coli  biofilms grown under different flow velocities shows no clear evidence of a mechanical-specific signaling response to increased hydrodynamic stress 166 . Instead, the differential transcriptomic analysis primarily identified genes associated with cellular micro-aerobic metabolism, indicating that biofilms grown under lower fluid dynamics experienced stronger low-oxygen stress compared to those grown under higher fluid dynamics 166 . These findings suggest that biofilms may indirectly modulate their local mechanical properties through regulation of their internal microchemical environment. Hart and Pavissich et al. also proposed that shear flow may preferentially remove loosely attached cells from the biofilm surface, potentially affecting the mechanical properties of the outer biofilm layer 76 , 161 .

In summary, although many factors have been shown to influence the mechanical properties of different types of biofilms, the nature and extent of these effects are likely to vary across species. Moreover, despite the observed correlations, the underlying mechanisms and regulatory pathways governing the coupled effects of EPS and cell density, external and internal chemical environments, and hydrodynamic conditions on biofilm mechanics remain incompletely understood, and quantitative relationships describing these effects are still lacking. This gap is partly attributable to the lack of experimental platforms capable of in situ and synchronous monitoring of gene expression, biofilm material composition and architecture, and their mechanical properties, which limits mechanistic understanding of these coupled processes. With the necessary data support provided by experimental approaches, multiphase coupled modeling frameworks are also essential for attributing and interpreting mechanical heterogeneity.

Nevertheless, precise characterization of the biofilm microenvironment and the physiological activities of individual cells form the foundation for understanding mechanical heterogeneity. Furthermore, the mechanical heterogeneity discussed above suggests that, when considering the direct impact of external mechanical forces, approaches that extend beyond homogeneous continuum deformation analyses are required. Models incorporating mechanical heterogeneity, fluid–structure interactions, and biofilm structural remodeling are necessary to capture the relevant physical processes. Taken together, the development of integrated and comprehensive microscale analytical platforms represents a key direction for advancing the study of biofilm mechanical heterogeneity.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Biofilms are composite biological materials formed through the ordered or disordered assembly of diverse components and undergo dynamic developmental processes. The evolution of biofilm architecture is strongly influenced by both global and local mechanical behaviors, while the resulting morphology and compositional distribution, in turn, modulate mechanical properties. A thorough understanding of biofilm architectural evolution requires dynamic, high-frequency, or continuous observation platforms to capture these coupled processes in real time. A defining feature of biofilms is their capacity for adaptive response to external stimuli through time-dependent feedback that spans molecular, cellular, and macroscopic scales. This multi-tiered regulation integrates chemical, physical, and biological processes, such as intermolecular bonding, water permeation, metabolic shifts, and phenotypic differentiation, that collectively shape biofilm composition and structure. Accurately characterizing these complex feedback demands comprehensive monitoring systems that can simultaneously probe biofilm architecture, physicochemical fields, and cellular activity. In parallel, multiphase and multiscale modeling frameworks are essential for disentangling the distinct contributions of biochemical, mechanical, and structural factors to emergent heterogeneity. Current understanding of biofilm mechano-chemical behavior and its underlying mechanisms is largely derived from modeling approaches combined with experimental validation. Advancing and refining these modeling frameworks is therefore crucial for deepening insight into biofilm function and performance.

At present, a major challenge in developing suitable platforms for mechanical study lies in reconciling intrinsic biofilm diversity with the compatibility of analytical theories. Biochemical traits and mechanical behaviors of microbial species can vary substantially, and overlapping material properties often make it difficult to isolate single variables in a controlled fashion. Nevertheless, extensive experimental evidence consistently reveals strong correlations between the micro- and macroscopic composition, structure, and mechanics of biofilms, highlighting cross-species trends and underlying principles. A bottom-up perspective aimed at uncovering these unifying mechanisms, therefore, holds great promise. Advances in microscale characterization now enable observation of local biofilm features with increasing precision, supporting the development of analytical and simulation models at molecular and cellular levels. Yet, a critical gap remains between discrete cell-based gel frameworks and continuum constitutive models. Achieving a more comprehensive understanding of how biofilm heterogeneity arises and how distinct components interact will be key to addressing this challenge. Furthermore, close integration between numerical simulations and experimental observations, with careful consideration of methodological and environmental discrepancies, will be essential. Ultimately, developing multiscale modeling frameworks that integrate both biochemical and mechanical factors will not only illuminate the synergistic mechanisms governing biofilm mechanics but also provide valuable guidance for controlling biofilm growth and function across diverse environments.
